questions.prompt: What typically takes up the largest share of a data science project's time?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Collecting, cleaning, and reshaping data

Cleaning and preparing data is consistently reported as the most time-consuming part of real-world data science work — often 60-80% of total effort.
keyPoints: Cleaning and preparing data is consistently reported as the most time-consuming part of real-world data science work — often 60-80% of total effort.

questions.prompt: Which pandas function reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: pd.read_csv()

`pd.read_csv()` is the standard way to load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame.
keyPoints: `pd.read_csv()` is the standard way to load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame.

questions.prompt: What does `df["total"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]` do?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Creates a new column called total holding the element-wise product of price and quantity

Assigning the result of an element-wise operation to a new column name both computes and stores it as a new column in the DataFrame.
keyPoints: Assigning the result of an element-wise operation to a new column name both computes and stores it as a new column in the DataFrame.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't outliers automatically be deleted from a dataset?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Some outliers represent the exact phenomenon you're trying to study, like fraud or rare events

An outlier might be a genuine, important observation (like a fraudulent transaction) rather than an error — deleting it without investigating could throw away the most important data point.
keyPoints: An outlier might be a genuine, important observation (like a fraudulent transaction) rather than an error — deleting it without investigating could throw away the most important data point.

questions.prompt: What is feature engineering?
questions.referenceAnswer: Feature engineering is the process of transforming or combining raw data into columns (features) that are more directly useful for analysis or modeling.
keyPoints: Feature engineering is the process of transforming or combining raw data into columns (features) that are more directly useful for analysis or modeling.

choices.text: Writing tests for a model
Creating new, more useful columns from existing raw data
Cleaning duplicate rows
Choosing which model architecture to use

questions.prompt: What's a downside of including too many irrelevant features in a model?
questions.referenceAnswer: Extra irrelevant or redundant features can drown out genuinely useful signal, slow down computation, and make the model more prone to memorizing noise rather than learning general patterns.
keyPoints: Extra irrelevant or redundant features can drown out genuinely useful signal, slow down computation, and make the model more prone to memorizing noise rather than learning general patterns.

choices.text: The model will refuse to train

It always improves accuracy
There is no real downside

questions.prompt: What does a scatter plot with points sloping upward from left to right suggest?
questions.referenceAnswer: An upward slope in a scatter plot suggests the two plotted variables tend to move in the same direction — often the visual signature of a positive correlation.
keyPoints: An upward slope in a scatter plot suggests the two plotted variables tend to move in the same direction — often the visual signature of a positive correlation.

choices.text: A negative relationship between the two variables
A positive relationship — as one variable increases, the other tends to increase too
No relationship at all
The data must be wrong

questions.prompt: Why is a chart with no accompanying code or data trail hard to trust?
questions.referenceAnswer: Reproducibility is what lets others (or future you) verify a result actually came from the stated process — without the underlying code and data, a chart is unverifiable.
keyPoints: Reproducibility is what lets others (or future you) verify a result actually came from the stated process — without the underlying code and data, a chart is unverifiable.

choices.text: Charts are inherently unreliable
No one can verify, rerun, or extend the analysis behind it — it's just a claim
Charts should never be used in reports
It's not actually a problem

questions.prompt: A model performs well offline but fails on newly collected data. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Check train/test leakage and time-based splits. Compare feature distributions and missing values. Fit preprocessing on training data only.
keyPoints: Check train/test leakage and time-based splits.
Compare feature distributions and missing values.
Fit preprocessing on training data only.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Fit preprocessing on training data only. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Fit preprocessing on training data only.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Check train/test leakage and time-based splits. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Check train/test leakage and time-based splits.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
